items.definition: Damage caused by insiders, on purpose or by mistake, including theft and unauthorised software.
items.examples: Copying the customer database to a USB before resigning; installing pirated software.
items.examTip: Insiders have legitimate access, so they are harder to detect. Say WHO did WHAT.
keyFacts: Deliberate (revenge, theft) or accidental, so an organisation must guard against honest mistakes as well as malice
Theft of equipment, data or licences, which insiders find easy because they already have access
Unauthorised software brings legal and malware risks: unlicensed copies break copyright and may hide malware

items.definition: Physical events, natural, accidental or deliberate, that damage IT systems and data.
items.examples: A burst pipe flooding a server room; arson; a power cut.
items.examTip: Justifies off-site backups and disaster recovery plans.
keyFacts: Fire, flood, power loss or terrorism can strike without warning, so they must be planned for
Destroys hardware and the data on it, so systems are down until both are replaced
Reduce with off-site backups, UPS and fire suppression, so data survives and systems keep running

items.definition: Poor habits and weak controls that make an organisation easier to attack.
items.examples: An unlocked server room; unescorted visitors; staff on dodgy download sites.
items.examTip: A human weakness: fix it with training and policy, not just technology.
keyFacts: Equipment not physically secured, so devices and data can simply be picked up and taken
Visitors not vetted, so an attacker can walk in posing as a contractor or delivery driver
Visiting untrustworthy websites can download malware onto work systems

items.term: Accidental Loss/Disclosure of Data or Credentials
items.definition: Data or logins exposed through human error rather than a deliberate attack.
items.examples: Emailing customer data to the wrong person; a password on a sticky note.
items.examTip: Root causes: negligence, poor training, not following procedures.
keyFacts: Human factors such as negligence and poor training cause it, e.g. emailing data to the wrong person
Worse with weak monitoring, because leaks go unnoticed and can't be stopped or reported in time
Usually a sign of a weak security culture, where staff don't see security as their responsibility

items.definition: Malicious code that attaches to a file and copies itself when the file is run.
items.examples: A macro virus in a Word document.
items.examTip: Know the types: boot sector, web script, macro, worm, rootkit, trojan, browser hijack, polymorphic.
keyFacts: Macro viruses hide in document macros, so opening an infected Word or Excel file runs them
Worm spreads across networks by itself, so it can infect many machines with no user action
Rootkit hides deep in the OS, so it is very hard for antivirus to detect or remove
Polymorphic viruses change their code to avoid detection, so signature-based antivirus misses them

items.definition: Software that secretly collects information about a user and sends it to a third party.
items.examples: A keylogger recording passwords.
items.examTip: Keylogger = records keystrokes to steal logins. A favourite exam term.
keyFacts: Keylogger records keystrokes, so passwords and card numbers can be stolen as they are typed
System monitor captures all activity, e.g. screenshots, emails and chats
Stalkerware tracks a phone's location, letting someone secretly follow a victim's movements
Tracking cookies follow browsing, building a profile of the user's interests for advertisers

items.definition: Software that displays or downloads adverts, from legitimate to deceptive.
items.examples: A free app showing pop-ups; unwanted software bundled with a download.
items.examTip: Not all adware is illegal: tell legitimate adware from abusive adware.
keyFacts: PUP (potentially unwanted program) is installed alongside other software, often without the user noticing
Legitimate adware funds free apps with the user's consent, so users get the app without paying
Deceptive adware can be illegal, because it installs without consent or tricks users into clicking

items.definition: Malware that locks or encrypts your data and demands payment to restore it.
items.examples: An encryptor scrambling all company files.
items.examTip: Best defence: tested OFFLINE backups, so you can restore without paying.
keyFacts: Encryptors scramble files so they can't be opened until a ransom is paid for the key
Lockers lock the whole screen, so the device can't be used at all
Leakware threatens to publish data, so even organisations with backups are pressured to pay
Defend with offline backups, patching and training, so data can be restored and fewer attacks get in

items.definition: Infected devices controlled remotely; many together form a botnet.
items.examples: Thousands of infected IoT devices flooding a website.
items.examTip: Botnets link malware to DDoS attacks: a common exam link.
keyFacts: Controlled remotely by the attacker, usually without the owner knowing their device is infected
Many bots together form a botnet, giving the attacker the power of thousands of devices
Used for spam and DDoS, because huge numbers of devices can send mail or flood a target at once

items.definition: Gaining unauthorised access to systems or data.
items.examples: A DDoS taking a website offline; changing records in a database.
items.examTip: DoS = one source; DDoS = many (a botnet).
keyFacts: DoS: one machine floods a target with traffic, so genuine users can't get through
DDoS: a botnet floods it from thousands of devices, so it is much harder to block than one source
Data theft and data tampering, so information is stolen or changed without anyone noticing
Cyberwarfare by states targets other countries' systems, e.g. to spy or disrupt

items.definition: Deliberately damaging or corrupting data, systems or infrastructure.
items.examples: Poisoning AI training data; hijacking connected machinery.
items.examTip: "Fakes" includes AI-generated images, video and audio.
keyFacts: Data poisoning, tampering and destruction, so the organisation can no longer trust or use its data
AI-generated fakes (e.g. deepfakes) can spread false information or trick staff
Hijacking machinery, vehicles or IoT devices, which can cause physical harm
Can target national infrastructure (power, water, transport), affecting whole populations

items.definition: Tricking people into giving away secure information instead of attacking technology.
items.examples: A fake bank email; a call pretending to be IT support.
items.examTip: Know the variants: phishing, vishing, smishing, whaling, spear phishing.
keyFacts: Phishing (email), vishing (phone) and smishing (text) all trick people into giving details or clicking links
Whaling targets senior staff and spear phishing targets one person, using research to seem convincing
Pretexting uses a made-up story (e.g. posing as IT support) to get information
Best defence is training, because these attacks target people, not technology

items.definition: Threats that involve physically reaching a secure area or device.
items.examples: Tailgating through a door; shoulder surfing a password.
items.examTip: Tailgating = following someone through a secure door. Learn this definition.
keyFacts: Area access by tailgating, forced entry or impersonation gets an attacker into restricted spaces
Device access through unattended devices, shoulder surfing or theft exposes data without any hacking
Devices in public places are most exposed, because anyone can watch or grab them

items.definition: The organisation can't operate or deliver its products and services.
items.examples: A production line stopped by ransomware; a website down so no orders.
items.examTip: Operational = the business can't function.
keyFacts: Lost production, because systems needed to make products or deliver services are down
Services unavailable, so customers can't buy, book or get support
Data unavailable, so staff can't do their jobs even if systems are running

items.definition: The money an incident costs: lost income, compensation and legal costs.
items.examples: GDPR fines; refunds to affected customers.
items.examTip: Split it into organisational costs, compensation and legal liability.
keyFacts: Lost profits and higher insurance, because sales stop and insurers see the organisation as riskier
Compensation and refunds to customers whose data or service was affected
Fines and legal fees, e.g. from the ICO under GDPR or from customers suing

items.definition: Damage to how customers and the public see the organisation.
items.examples: Angry reviews on social media after a breach.
items.examTip: Often the longest-lasting impact: lost trust is hard to rebuild.
keyFacts: Loss of customer trust, so customers move to competitors
Poor reviews online, which put off new customers
Lower reputation scores, which can lose contracts with partners and investors

items.definition: Theft or exposure of an organisation's valuable ideas and secrets.
items.examples: A rival stealing a new product design.
items.examTip: Destroys competitive advantage even with no personal data involved.
keyFacts: Product designs stolen, so competitors can copy them without the development cost
Testing and development data exposed, losing years of research
Strategy and trade secrets leaked, so the organisation loses its competitive advantage

items.definition: The National Cyber Security Centre: the UK authority publishing threat reports and advice.
items.examples: Checking the NCSC site for the latest ransomware advisory.
items.examTip: NCSC = UK. Use it because threats keep changing.
keyFacts: UK government body, so its advice is authoritative for UK organisations
Publishes threat reports and malware analysis, so organisations know what attacks to expect
Advisories and guidance give practical steps to protect systems

items.definition: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which issues security standards and advisories.
items.examples: Following NIST guidance on password policy.
items.examTip: NIST = the US equivalent of the NCSC.
keyFacts: US standards body whose security standards are used worldwide
News and advisories warn organisations about new vulnerabilities
Widely used security frameworks give organisations a structured way to manage risk

items.definition: A non-profit whose Top 10 lists the most critical web application security risks.
items.examples: Checking a website for SQL injection using the OWASP Top 10.
items.examTip: Used in penetration testing: link the two.
keyFacts: Focuses on web application security, the risks to websites and online services
Top 10 is updated regularly, so it reflects the latest attack trends
Used as a checklist for pen testing, so testers check the most common weaknesses first

items.definition: Weaknesses in network set-up, especially open firewall ports and external storage.
items.examples: An exposed open port; malware arriving on a USB stick.
items.examTip: Port types: well-known (e.g. 80 for HTTP), registered, dynamic/private. Open ports = risk.
keyFacts: Three port categories: well-known (0–1023), registered and dynamic, so admins know which should be open
Risks include open ports, spoofing and DoS, because every open port is a way in for attackers
External storage can bring in malware, e.g. an infected USB stick plugged into a network PC

items.definition: Weaknesses in how permissions, passwords and accounts are managed.
items.examples: Everyone having admin rights; not disabling a leaver's account.
items.examTip: Password policy points (length, characters, reuse, age) are easy marks.
keyFacts: Permissions (read, write, execute, modify) set too widely let staff change data they shouldn't
Password policy (length, characters, reuse, age) makes passwords harder to guess or crack
Lock unused accounts and remove leavers, so old logins can't be used by attackers or ex-staff
Browser auto-fill is a risk, because anyone using the device can log in with saved passwords

items.definition: Weaknesses from untrustworthy, outdated or badly made software.
items.examples: Pirated software with a backdoor; an unpatched web app open to SQL injection.
items.examTip: Zero-day = a new flaw with no patch yet.
keyFacts: Safe downloads: trusted source, HTTPS, malware scan and hash check, so the file hasn't been tampered with
Illegal copies get no updates, so their security flaws are never fixed
Zero-day exploits attack flaws the vendor doesn't know about yet, so no patch exists
SQL injection and missing patches let attackers read or change databases through badly written code

items.definition: Weaknesses in the OS and its interfaces, usually from being outdated or misconfigured.
items.examples: An unsupported version of Windows.
items.examTip: Unsupported software no longer gets security patches.
keyFacts: Unsupported versions no longer get security updates, so new flaws stay open forever
Missing patches leave known flaws open, which attackers actively scan for
Wrong security settings (e.g. default admin passwords) make systems easy to break into

items.definition: Phones depend on their manufacturer (OEM) for updates, so they can be left unpatched.
items.examples: An old Android phone that no longer gets updates.
items.examTip: Updates may be slow or stop entirely, leaving known flaws open.
keyFacts: Updates come from the manufacturer (OEM), not just the OS maker, so patches can arrive late
Older devices stop getting updates, even though people keep using them for years
Known flaws stay unpatched, so attackers can exploit them on those devices

items.definition: Weaknesses that allow theft of, or physical access to, equipment holding data.
items.examples: A stolen laptop; a badly secured restricted area.
items.examTip: Link to physical security measures.
keyFacts: Theft of devices holding data, so unencrypted data can be read by whoever takes them
Poor security for restricted areas, so intruders can reach servers and network equipment

items.definition: Weaknesses in how people actually use systems day to day.
items.examples: Sharing a login; a process that lets data leave unchecked.
items.examTip: Human weaknesses: fixed by training, policy and better processes.
keyFacts: Leaks, deliberate or accidental, expose data even when the technology is secure
Sharing security details (e.g. passwords) means anyone could be using that account
Flawed processes (e.g. no check before sending data) make mistakes likely

items.definition: Security risks specific to cloud services and IoT devices.
items.examples: A misconfigured cloud store exposing data; a hijacked IoT camera.
items.examTip: Learn several IoT risks: default passwords, no encryption, no patches, always listening.
keyFacts: Cloud: wrong settings, third-party access and reliance on the provider can expose data or cut off access
IoT: weak encryption, default passwords and no patches make devices easy to hack
IoT: set up by non-IT staff and always listening, so insecure devices can join the network unnoticed

items.definition: Where to find up-to-date information on known vulnerabilities.
items.examples: A manufacturer's website; a professional security forum.
items.examTip: Three sources: manufacturer, professional forums, specialist third-party sites.
keyFacts: Manufacturer's website lists patches and known issues for its own products
IT and security forums share experiences and fixes from other professionals
Specialist third-party sites (e.g. CVE databases) track vulnerabilities across many products

items.definition: The routes an attacker uses to reach a system.
items.examples: Attacking over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth; exploiting a router.
items.examTip: An attack vector is the "way in".
keyFacts: Wireless (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, NFC, RFID) can be attacked from outside the building
Internet connections expose systems to attackers anywhere in the world
Internal devices (router, switch, access point) give control of traffic if compromised

items.definition: Tools that find weaknesses in systems before attackers do.
items.examples: A port scanner; a website vulnerability scanner.
items.examTip: Know the named tools.
keyFacts: Port scanner and network mapper show which devices and open ports exist, revealing ways in
Registry checker finds suspicious or wrong settings in Windows that malware may have changed
Website vulnerability scanner tests sites for common flaws like SQL injection
Phishing simulations test users, showing who needs more training

items.definition: An outside expert reviewing system designs before they are built.
items.examples: A consultancy reviewing and certifying a new network design.
items.examTip: Shows due diligence and gives independent certification.
keyFacts: Done before implementation, so design flaws are fixed before they cost money to change
Shows due diligence, proving the organisation took reasonable care over security
Third-party certification gives customers and partners confidence the system is secure

items.definition: Authorised simulated attacks to find weak spots, ending in a report.
items.examples: A pen tester trying to break into a network.
items.examTip: Real attack techniques used with permission. Links to OWASP.
keyFacts: Uses a range of attack techniques, so it finds weaknesses a real attacker would use
Checks against known lists (OWASP Top 10), so the most common weaknesses are covered
Produces a report listing weaknesses and fixes, so the organisation knows what to do next

items.definition: Managing risk without adding security controls: transfer, avoid or accept it.
items.examples: Buying cyber insurance; stopping a risky activity.
items.examTip: Three options: transfer, avoid, accept.
keyFacts: Transfer the risk to someone else, e.g. insurance, so they bear the cost if it happens
Avoid it by stopping the activity, so the risk no longer exists
Accept a small risk when protecting against it would cost more than the likely loss

items.definition: Law protecting personal data and people's privacy rights.
items.examples: Getting consent before collecting data; reporting a breach within 72 hours.
items.examTip: GDPR = personal data and privacy. Don't mix it up with the Computer Misuse Act.
keyFacts: Protects personal data and privacy, giving people control over their information
Applies to stored and transferred data, so data must be protected at rest and in transit
Covers anything that identifies a person, e.g. name, email, IP address or photo

items.definition: Law making unauthorised access to, or modification of, computers and data a crime.
items.examples: Hacking into a system you have no permission to use.
items.examTip: Computer Misuse Act = unauthorised access and modification.
keyFacts: Unauthorised access is an offence, even if nothing is changed or stolen
Changing data without permission is an offence, e.g. altering or deleting records
Covers hacking and creating malware, so writing or spreading viruses is a crime

items.definition: The core rules for processing personal data under GDPR.
items.examples: Collecting the minimum data, keeping it accurate, deleting it when done.
items.examTip: Lawful/fair/transparent, set purpose, accurate, minimal, minimum time, secure.
keyFacts: Lawful, fair and transparent, so people know how their data is used
Limited purpose and accurate, so data is only used for the reason it was collected and kept correct
Minimum data for the minimum time, so less is at risk if there is a breach
Kept confidential and intact, so data is secured against loss, theft and damage

items.definition: The valid legal reasons an organisation can have for processing personal data.
items.examples: Payroll under "contract"; medical data under "vital interest".
items.examTip: Six bases: consent, contract, legitimate interest, vital interest, legal requirement, public interest.
keyFacts: Consent or a contract, e.g. a customer agrees, or the data is needed to deliver their order
Legitimate interest or vital interest, e.g. fraud prevention, or protecting someone's life
Legal requirement or public interest, e.g. sharing data with HMRC, or tasks for the public good

items.definition: The rights people have over their own personal data.
items.examples: Asking for a copy of your data or for it to be deleted.
items.examTip: Access, be informed, correct/erase/restrict, object, portability, no solely automated decisions.
keyFacts: Right to access and be informed, so people can see what is held and why
Right to correct, erase or restrict, so wrong data is fixed and unwanted data removed
Right to object and to portability, so people can stop some uses and take their data elsewhere
Not subject to solely automated decisions, so a person can ask for a human to review the decision

items.definition: Measures that physically protect equipment, sites and restricted areas.
items.examples: Card entry; fingerprint scanners; CCTV; locked server cabinets.
items.examTip: Group them: locks, card entry, biometrics, surveillance, training.
keyFacts: Locks, mechanical or electronic, stop unauthorised people entering rooms
Card entry (NFC, RFID, QR, chip) controls and logs who goes where
Biometrics (fingerprint, iris, face, voice) can't be lent or lost like a card
CCTV, guards and alarms deter intruders and provide evidence

items.definition: Copying data so it can be restored after loss, corruption or attack.
items.examples: A weekly full backup plus daily incrementals stored off-site.
items.examTip: Full, incremental (since last backup), differential (since last full). RAID is NOT a backup.
keyFacts: Types: full, differential and incremental, which trade backup speed against restore speed
On-site, off-site and cloud: off-site and cloud copies survive a fire or flood at the main site
RAID and archiving are not backups, because RAID copies deletions and corruption instantly
Restore a file, an image or the whole system, depending on how much was lost

items.definition: Software that detects, blocks and removes malware using signatures and heuristics.
items.examples: Quarantining a suspicious file.
items.examTip: Signatures catch known malware; heuristics catch new behaviour.
keyFacts: Signature scanning finds known threats by matching them against a database
Heuristics spot suspicious behaviour, so new malware without a signature can still be caught
File integrity checks spot changed system files, which can be a sign of infection
Responses (warn, block, quarantine, delete) stop the threat spreading

items.definition: Hardware or software that filters traffic using rules to block unauthorised access.
items.examples: Blocking inbound traffic on every port except those needed.
items.examTip: Inbound and outbound rules; packet filtering; application awareness.
keyFacts: Packet filtering and inspection check each packet against rules, blocking anything not allowed
Application-layer awareness lets it understand traffic from specific apps, so it can block risky ones
Inbound and outbound rules stop attacks coming in and data leaking out
Filtering by address blocks known malicious IP addresses

items.definition: Checking users are who they claim to be, often using more than one factor.
items.examples: Password + USB security key; an authenticator app code.
items.examTip: Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence, plus location and behaviour. A USB key = possession.
keyFacts: Single-factor uses one check, while multi-factor needs two or more, so a stolen password isn't enough
Factors are knowledge (password), possession (phone or token) and inherence (fingerprint)
Tokens (USB key, contactless card, code generator) prove the user has a physical item
Certificate-based authentication uses a digital certificate on the device, so no password is needed

items.definition: Methods that control which users can access which resources.
items.examples: Finance can open accounts but not HR files.
items.examTip: DAC: owners control files. Role-based: by job. Rule-based: rules per user.
keyFacts: DAC lets users control their own resources, which is flexible but less secure
Role-based access is set by job role, so new staff get the right access automatically
Rule-based access applies rules to each user, e.g. only during working hours
Applies to apps, files and devices, so every resource is protected

items.definition: Hardware-based security, e.g. a TPM chip, that adds protection but reduces user control.
items.examples: A TPM checking the system is trusted before start-up.
items.examTip: Benefit: more security. Drawback: less user control and privacy.
keyFacts: Adds another layer of protection, e.g. a TPM chip storing encryption keys in hardware
Less user control, privacy and anonymity, because the hardware enforces what can run

items.definition: Measures that protect devices and help locate, lock or wipe lost ones.
items.examples: "Find my device"; remotely wiping a stolen phone.
items.examTip: Remote lock/wipe and timed lockout are strong answers.
keyFacts: GPS and tracking software help locate lost or stolen devices
Screen locks after time or failed logins, so an unattended device can't be used
Wipe after too many failed attempts, so a thief can't keep guessing the passcode
Remote lock and wipe, so data on a lost device is protected even if it isn't found

items.definition: Encrypting stored data so a stolen device or drive is unreadable.
items.examples: Full-disk encryption on a laptop.
items.examTip: Protects data "at rest": vital for lost or stolen devices.
keyFacts: Safe password storage (hashed, not plain text), so stolen password files are useless
Digital Rights Management (DRM) stops copyrighted content being copied or shared
File, folder, disk and device encryption make stolen data unreadable

items.definition: Encrypting data in transit so it can't be read if intercepted.
items.examples: HTTPS; VPNs; end-to-end encrypted messaging.
items.examTip: Symmetric = one shared key (AES, fast). Asymmetric = public/private pair (RSA).
keyFacts: Symmetric uses one secret key (e.g. AES), so it is fast, but the key must be shared securely
Asymmetric uses public and private keys (e.g. RSA), so no secret key has to be shared
Used in VPNs, HTTPS and TOR, so traffic can't be read as it crosses the internet
End-to-end encryption in messaging means only sender and recipient can read messages

items.definition: Precautions that protect a wireless network from unauthorised access.
items.examples: WPA3; hiding the SSID; MAC filtering; changing default passwords.
items.examTip: MAC addresses can be spoofed, so MAC filtering is only medium security.
keyFacts: MAC filtering and hiding the SSID add small obstacles, but both are easily bypassed by spoofing or scanning
Use WPA2/WPA3, so traffic is strongly encrypted
Attacks include Evil Twin, piggybacking and sniffing, which steal access or data
Change defaults and use VPNs and firewalls, so known default passwords can't be used

items.definition: Building security in from the start rather than adding it later.
items.examples: Designing with least privilege and assuming attackers will try.
items.examTip: Expect attacks, least privilege, don't rely on secrecy, follow standards (ISO 27000).
keyFacts: Expect attacks, so defences are designed in from the start, not added after a breach
Least privilege gives users only the access they need, limiting damage if an account is compromised
Don't rely on secrecy: a system should stay secure even if attackers know how it works
Follow ISO 27000 standards, so security meets a recognised international benchmark
